title: AI Music Producer
content_html:
Course Overview

AI Music Producer is a two-session deep dive into modern music-making, where students act as recording artists, producers, and graphic designers all at once. Using AI generation tools like Suno, real audio editing in Audacity, and AI image generation for cover art, students learn that "AI music" is not a single click of a button — it is a creative pipeline that involves songwriting structure, critical listening, remixing, arranging, and branding, just like a professional studio.

The course arc moves from composing to producing. In Session 1 (Compose), students learn the anatomy of a song — verse, chorus, bridge — and use that knowledge to write strong prompts and lyrics for AI music generators across multiple genres, then practice remixing and layering AI-generated clips into something more polished than a single generation. In Session 2 (Produce), students bring their own voice into the mix (literally), mix multiple AI stems together in Audacity, generate custom album art with an AI image tool, and assemble everything into a finished EP that gets "released" on a shared class playlist.

The take-home is a complete 3-track EP with custom album art — a real, listenable, shareable body of work that each student (or pair) can play for family and friends, post to a class showcase, or keep as a portfolio piece.

Learning Outcomes

  • Can explain and identify song structure (verse, chorus, bridge, intro/outro) in a piece of music
  • Can write effective style and lyric prompts for an AI music generator (Suno), including genre, tempo, mood, and structural tags
  • Can generate, evaluate, and select the best of multiple AI-generated takes ("audition and curate" workflow)
  • Can layer and remix two or more audio clips into a single arranged track
  • Can record, trim, and mix a spoken/sung voice track alongside AI-generated instrumentals in Audacity
  • Can write effective image prompts for an AI image generator (DALL·E / Bing Image Creator) to produce cohesive album art
  • Can assemble and present a finished multi-track EP with a tracklist, cover art, and short artist statement

Materials Master List

Session Plans

Session 1: Compose — Genres, Song Structure, Remix & Layer

Objectives

  • Identify and explain the parts of a song: intro, verse, chorus, bridge, outro
  • Write structured prompts and lyrics to generate a full song in Suno across at least two genres
  • Generate multiple takes, select the best clips, and combine them into one longer remixed arrangement

Timing (90 minutes)

  • 0:00–0:10 — Welcome, course goal reveal ("you're making a real EP"), quick poll of favourite genres
  • 0:10–0:20 — Mini-lesson: song structure, using the reference sheet and a familiar song example
  • 0:20–0:30 — Facilitator live demo: generate one song in Suno from scratch, narrating every choice
  • 0:30–0:45 — Guided practice: students set up Suno accounts and generate their first structured song (Track 1 of the EP)
  • 0:45–0:60 — Genre exploration: each pair generates the same lyric idea in a second, different genre
  • 0:60–0:75 — Remix & layer exercise: combine two takes into one longer arrangement
  • 0:75–0:85 — Independent refinement time; facilitator circulates
  • 0:85–0:90 — Save/export everything to the shared Drive folder, preview Session 2

Step-by-step

  1. Open with: "Today you're not just clicking 'generate music' — you're a songwriter and producer deciding what makes a song good." Ask: "What are the parts of your favourite song?" Collect answers on the whiteboard.
  2. Hand out the Song Structure reference card. Walk through each part out loud using a well-known song (e.g. a current Afrobeat or pop hit most students know) — point out where the verse ends and chorus begins by clapping on the beat change.
  3. Project your screen. Log into a demo Suno account live. Show the two modes: Simple mode (type a short description, AI writes everything) and Custom mode (you supply style tags AND full lyrics with structure tags). Explain you will always use Custom mode in this course because it gives control over structure.
  4. Generate a demo track live using the exact example prompt below (see Build Detail). Narrate your thinking: "I'm setting the tempo to 110 because I want it upbeat, and I'm tagging [Chorus] so the AI knows to make that part catchy and repeat the melody."
  5. Play both of the 2 generated versions Suno produces. Ask the class to vote on which is better and why. This models the "audition and curate" skill they will use all day.
  6. Pairs log into their pre-created Suno account. Give them 5 minutes to brainstorm an EP theme as a class discussion prompt (e.g. "My City", "Superhero Origin Story", "Robot Uprising", "Friendship") — every student's 3 tracks should loosely share this theme so the EP feels cohesive.
  7. Guided practice: students draft their Track 1 lyrics on paper first (structure tags + at least 4 lines per section), then enter Custom mode and generate. Facilitator moves table to table checking that lyrics include [Verse], [Chorus], and at minimum one more section.
  8. Genre exploration: keeping the same lyrics, students change ONLY the style tag to a completely different genre and regenerate. Compare the two — discuss how genre changes mood even with identical words.
  9. Remix & layer exercise: introduce Suno's "Extend" feature (continues a song from a chosen timestamp in a new style/section) and show how to download two separate generated clips as MP3/WAV. Demonstrate dragging both into a rough timeline mentally — this sets up Session 2's real mixing work.
  10. Independent time: students finalize Track 1, download the best version, and rename the file clearly (e.g. GroupName_Track1_MyCity.mp3). Files get uploaded to their group subfolder in the Class Label Drive.
  11. Close with a 2-minute "sneak peek" — 2 volunteer pairs play 15 seconds of their favourite generation to the room.

Build detail

Tool & setup: Suno (suno.com), free account, Custom mode. Pre-create pair accounts before the session using a shared login sheet with username/password taped inside each laptop lid or written on a card per pair.

Workflow:

  1. Log in → click "Create" → toggle to Custom Mode.
  2. In the "Style of Music" field, enter a style tag describing genre, tempo, instrumentation, and mood.
  3. In the "Lyrics" field, write structured lyrics using square-bracket section tags: [Intro], [Verse 1], [Chorus], [Verse 2], [Bridge], [Outro].
  4. Click Generate — Suno produces 2 versions (~2 minutes each). Listen to both fully with headphones.
  5. Pick the stronger one, click the three-dot menu → Download → MP3 (or WAV for higher quality if time allows).

Exact example prompt (facilitator demo):

Style of Music: Uptempo Afro-pop, 108 BPM, warm analog synths, talking drum percussion, bright female lead vocal, joyful and energetic, festival atmosphere

Lyrics:
[Intro]
(Talking drum roll, crowd cheer sample)

[Verse 1]
Matatu horns are calling out my name
Nairobi mornings never feel the same
Dust on my shoes, sun on my face
This city's rhythm, I can't erase

[Chorus]
This is my city, this is my sound
Feet on the ground, heart lifting up now
Every corner got a story to tell
Nairobi calling, and I know it well

[Verse 2]
Green hills whisper, matatus roar
Every street corner's an open door
From Kibera beats to Karen's calm
This city holds me, this city's home

[Bridge]
(Half-time breakdown, vocal ad-libs, "oh oh oh")

[Chorus]
This is my city, this is my sound
Feet on the ground, heart lifting up now
Every corner got a story to tell
Nairobi calling, and I know it well

[Outro]
(Fade with talking drum and crowd ambience)

Second-genre example (same lyrics, new style tag, for the genre exploration step):

Style of Music: Lo-fi hip-hop, 78 BPM, dusty vinyl crackle, mellow jazz piano chords, soft rain ambience, laid-back and dreamy mood

What a good result looks like: a track roughly 1:30–2:30 long where the chorus melody is clearly more "hooky"/repeated than the verses, the mood matches the requested style tag, and there is an audible difference between the intro/verse energy and the chorus energy. Vocals should be reasonably intelligible (not required to match lyrics word-for-word — that's normal for AI music).

Testing/iteration: if a generation sounds muddy, too slow, or doesn't match the mood, tell students to keep the lyrics fixed and change ONE variable at a time in the style tag (tempo, instrument, or mood word) and regenerate — this teaches controlled experimentation rather than random re-rolling.

Checks for understanding

  • "Point to the reference card — where does the chorus usually repeat in a song, and why do you think that matters?"
  • "What's one word in your style tag that changed the whole feel of your song when you edited it?"
  • "Why did we write lyrics with [Verse]/[Chorus] tags instead of just typing 'make me a pop song'?"

Common mistakes & fixes

MistakeFix
Students write lyrics with no section tags, so Suno generates one continuous blob with no structurePause and require every group to have at least [Verse], [Chorus] tags visible before hitting Generate — check tables physically
Style tag is a single vague word like "cool music"Give the sentence starter: "[Genre], [tempo] BPM, [1 instrument], [1 mood word]" and require all four before generating
Students regenerate 8+ times chasing "perfect," running out of timeSet a rule: 2 generations per prompt attempt, pick the better one, move on — perfection comes in Session 2's mixing stage
Two students on shared account both editing at once causes lost workAssign clear roles per pair each round — one types prompt, one operates mouse/clicks generate — and swap roles halfway
File not downloaded/saved before time runs outBuild a hard "download and rename now" checkpoint into the schedule at 0:75 rather than leaving it open-ended

Session 2: Produce — Mix, Voice, Album Art & Release

Objectives

  • Mix multiple AI-generated tracks and a recorded voice clip together in Audacity
  • Generate cohesive album cover art using an AI image tool with a well-structured prompt
  • Assemble a finished 3-track EP with art and tracklist, and publish it to the class playlist

Timing (90 minutes)

  • 0:00–0:10 — Recap Session 1, reveal today's goal: "By the end of today your EP is finished and released"
  • 0:10–0:25 — Audacity setup and import walkthrough (facilitator demo + guided practice)
  • 0:25–0:40 — Voice recording session in rotating stations
  • 0:40–0:55 — Mixing: layering, trimming, fades, exporting final tracks
  • 0:55–0:70 — Album art creation with Bing Image Creator (DALL·E 3)
  • 0:70–0:80 — EP assembly: folder structure, tracklist doc, final naming
  • 0:80–0:90 — "Release" upload to class playlist + listening party kickoff

Step-by-step

  1. Recap: play one strong example clip from Session 1 saved in the Drive folder. Ask the room what genre/section it is.
  2. Explain today's factory-line: Mix → Art → Release. Draw this on the board as a 3-step pipeline they'll each move through.
  3. Open Audacity live on the projector. Show the interface: Tracks panel, Timeline, Play/Record/Stop buttons, Export menu. Demonstrate File → Import → Audio to bring in a Suno MP3 as Track 1.
  4. Demonstrate adding a second track (their Session 1 Track 1 alternate genre clip or a new Track 2 generation) below it — show how Audacity stacks tracks so they play simultaneously, and how to drag one track left/right on the timeline to offset when it starts (e.g. instrumental starts, then vocals/second layer enters 8 seconds later).
  5. Show the Selection Tool: click-drag to select a region, Ctrl+X (or Cmd+X) to cut an unwanted section (e.g. trim a boring intro), and Effect → Fade In / Fade Out on a selected region for smooth transitions.
  6. Introduce voice recording: explain today they'll record ONE spoken or sung element to make the EP personal — options: a spoken intro ("You're listening to [EP name], by [names]"), an ad-lib hook, or a short rap verse over an instrumental section.
  7. Set up 1–2 quiet recording corners with the USB mic or a laptop's built-in mic. Rotate pairs through in small groups while others continue mixing. Demonstrate: click the red Record button in Audacity, count in "3-2-1", speak/sing, click Stop, then Play to check the take, re-record if needed.
  8. Guided mixing: students layer their recorded voice track under/over their chosen instrumental section, adjust volume with the track's gain slider so the voice sits clearly on top (not buried), and trim/fade so the final track is a clean 1:30–2:30 length.
  9. Export: File → Export → Export as MP3. Name file consistently: GroupName_Track#_Title.mp3. Repeat this whole pipeline mentally for Tracks 2 and 3 (these can be lightly touched Session 1 exports if time is short — the priority is that at least ONE track has full voice + layering treatment).
  10. Album art: move to Bing Image Creator (or ChatGPT if a Plus account is available). Demonstrate writing an image prompt describing the EP's mood/theme, generating 4 options, and picking the strongest, cohesive one.
  11. EP assembly: in the group's Drive subfolder, create the final structure: an "EP" folder containing Track1.mp3, Track2.mp3, Track3.mp3, CoverArt.png, and a simple Tracklist.txt with EP title, artist name(s), and one sentence describing each track.
  12. Release: students drag their finished EP folder into the shared "Class Label" master folder. Facilitator opens the master folder on the projector and plays a track from each EP in turn as the listening party.

Build detail

Tools & setup: Audacity 3.x (pre-installed and tested on every device), a shared USB or laptop microphone at 1–2 stations, Bing Image Creator (bing.com/create, powered by DALL·E 3, logged in with the pre-created Microsoft account), and the shared Class Label Google Drive folder from Session 1.

Mixing workflow, step by step:

  1. Open Audacity → File → Import → Audio → select the Suno instrumental MP3 (this becomes Track 1 in the Audacity project).
  2. Repeat Import for a second AI clip if layering two instrumentals, OR skip to voice recording if only layering voice + one instrumental.
  3. Click the red Record button to add a new voice track; count in and record directly into the same project so it lines up with the existing timeline.
  4. Use the Time Shift Tool (double-headed arrow icon) to drag the voice track left/right so it starts at the right moment (e.g. right as the chorus tag would begin).
  5. Select the voice track → Effect menu → Fade In (first 1 second) and Fade Out (last 1 second) to avoid clicks/pops.
  6. Use the track's volume slider (top-left of each track) to balance levels — voice should be clearly audible over instrumental, not overpowering it or buried under it. Good rule of thumb: instrumental slightly quieter than voice during spoken sections.
  7. File → Export → Export as MP3 → save into the group's Drive-synced folder.

Exact example voice-recording scripts (offer as choices):

Spoken intro option:
"You're listening to MY CITY, an EP by [Student Names]. Track one: Nairobi Calling. Turn it up."

Ad-lib/hook option (spoken rhythmically over the beat):
"Nairobi! (echo) Nairobi! (echo) This is our sound, this is our home."

Short rap verse option (16 bars, write on paper first, then record):
"Wake up in the city where the matatus fly,
Green hills all around us, touching the sky,
We got the beat, we got the sound,
Nairobi rising, we don't back down..."

Exact example album art prompt (Bing Image Creator / DALL·E 3):

Album cover art for an EP titled "MY CITY". Vibrant flat-illustration style digital art of the Nairobi skyline at golden hour, blended with musical elements like sound waves and a vinyl record silhouette in the sky, warm orange and teal color palette, energetic and joyful mood, square 1:1 composition, no text or words in the image

What a good result looks like: a finished track where the voice is clearly audible and timed intentionally (not randomly plopped in), a smooth start/end with fades (no abrupt cuts), consistent volume between elements, and cover art that visually matches the EP's stated theme/mood with a clean square composition and no garbled AI text (explicitly tell the tool "no text" since AI image generators struggle with legible words).

Testing/iteration: after export, play the finished MP3 back through the class speakers (not just laptop speakers) — ask "can everyone hear the voice clearly?" If not, reopen the Audacity project, adjust volume sliders, re-export. For art, generate at least 3 image variations and have partners vote before locking in the final cover — mirrors real creative direction.

Checks for understanding

  • "Why did we fade the audio in and out instead of just cutting it sharply?"
  • "What happens to your mix if the voice track volume is louder/quieter than the instrumental — try it and tell me which sounds better and why."
  • "Why did we tell the image generator 'no text' in the prompt?"

Common mistakes & fixes

MistakeFix
Voice recording is too quiet or too loud compared to instrumentalUse the per-track volume slider in Audacity, not the system volume — demonstrate side-by-side comparison at two slider settings
Recorded take has laughing, "umm," or long silence at the startTeach the "3-2-1 silent countdown, then speak" habit; trim dead air with the Selection Tool + Delete before exporting
Tracks layered with jarring, abrupt starts/stopsAlways apply Fade In/Fade Out (Effect menu) to every clip edge before export
Album art prompt is too vague, resulting in generic or mismatched artRequire every prompt to include: subject, style, color palette, mood, composition — check against this checklist before generating
Group runs out of time before finishing all 3 tracksPre-agree that Track 1 gets full mix+voice treatment, and Tracks 2–3 can be the strongest Session 1 exports with just a fade in/out applied — priority is a complete, released EP over three equally-polished tracks

Assessment & Showcase

Assess students continuously rather than with a written test — this is a studio, not a classroom. Use this simple rubric while circulating in both sessions:

CriterionEmergingProficientExcelling
Song structureLyrics have no clear sectionsLyrics include at least verse + chorus tagsFull structure used (intro/verse/chorus/bridge/outro) with intentional pacing
Prompting skillVague one-word style tagsStyle tags include genre, tempo, instrument, moodIterates deliberately, changing one variable at a time to shape the sound
Mixing & voiceNo voice track or badly balanced volumeVoice recorded, roughly balanced, some fades usedVoice timed intentionally, levels balanced, clean fades throughout
Album artGeneric image unrelated to EP themeArt matches genre/mood of EPArt and EP title/theme feel like a cohesive, professional release
CollaborationOne partner does all the workRoles shared across the sessionBoth partners can explain every decision made in the final EP

Run the final 15–20 minutes of Session 2 as a Listening Party / Release Show: connect a laptop to the class speakers, open the shared "Class Label" Drive folder, and play one track from each group's EP in turn while projecting their cover art. Before each play, have the group give a 15-second "artist statement" — EP title, genre choices, and one thing they're proud of. "Done" means: a folder in the Class Label Drive containing 3 exported audio files, one piece of cover art, and a short tracklist document, with at least one track featuring the student's own recorded voice mixed in.

Extension & Home Challenges

  • Easy: Create a bonus 4th track in a genre the group hasn't tried yet (e.g. if the EP was Afro-pop/lo-fi, try amapiano or reggae), using full structure tags and at least two generations compared before choosing the final one.
  • Medium: Record a full 16-bar rap or sung verse (not just a hook or ad-lib) written entirely by the student, mix it over an AI instrumental in Audacity with proper volume balancing and fades, and add it as a fourth "bonus track" or remix of an existing track.
  • Hard: Turn the EP into a mini visual "era": generate a cohesive cover art AND two additional single-cover images that share the same color palette, character style, or visual motif as the main album art, then write a one-paragraph "liner notes" artist statement explaining the EP's story/theme and how the visuals connect to the music — assemble all of it (3 tracks, 3 pieces of art, liner notes) into one shareable folder or simple slideshow to present to family.
